magnesium-l-threonate.claim_note: Both trials are brand-funded. Hausenblas found ring-measured deep and REM gains plus subjective benefits. Lopresti found one self-rated sleep measure improved, with no ring-measured sleep change. The summary describes both accurately.
magnesium-l-threonate.tier_note: Under the rules, brand-funded studies count as none, so N is correct even though both are placebo-controlled RCTs.
magnesium-l-threonate.rules_note: An N row that is kept only when the person's own and loved, and cleared when borrowed, weak, overlapping or unused, is consistent with the rules. It is not a cost row.
magnesium-l-threonate.words_note: The fits_instead line implies magnesium glycinate is a proven, cheaper sleep aid. Glycinate's sleep evidence in healthy adults is also thin, so the wording should be softened (e.g., 'if you want magnesium, a cheaper form like glycinate'). The summary could also note that both samples had self-reported poor sleep.
magnesium-l-threonate.one_line: The N tier and the summary are right, but reword the glycinate suggestion so it doesn't imply that form is proven to help sleep.

sources.note: The summary confirms transdermal magnesium is scientifically unsupported; the 'tiny, uncontrolled or unpublished' detail and the claim that no study tested sleep come from the paraphrase or the row, not the abstract.

magnesium-spray-oil-transdermal.claim_note: One independent review calls skin absorption unsupported; the sleep part is not addressed in the summary, so 'none has tested sleep' rests on the row's own statement.
magnesium-spray-oil-transdermal.tier_note: Small, uncontrolled studies of uptake exist, so D could also be argued, but D and N behave identically here: both can be cleared when borrowed and unloved.
magnesium-spray-oil-transdermal.rules_note: Keeping it when THEIRS and LOVED, and clearing it via BORROWED_WEAK or FORM_NOT_ABSORBED, fits a no-evidence, benefit-direction row.
magnesium-spray-oil-transdermal.words_note: The summary is accurate. fits_instead should not imply that oral glycinate helps sleep in healthy adults, since that evidence is weak too; the wording 'if the magnesium matters' keeps it hedged.
magnesium-spray-oil-transdermal.one_line: This row is sound: magnesium spray has no good evidence of absorbing through skin or helping sleep, so it is fine to suggest dropping it unless the person loves the ritual.

sources.note: Night-waking benefit was 2 of 3 trials and not pooled, and PSQI pooling had I² 88%; the paraphrase notes heterogeneity but the row's summary does not.
No published summary; judged from the paraphrase only, which flags ragweed-family allergy and a possible warfarin interaction.

chamomile-tea.claim_note: Two independent meta-analyses show improved subjective sleep quality but no improvement in duration, with small, heterogeneous trials in mixed healthy and patient groups. The 'mostly extracts, few tea trials' point is plausible but not stated in either summary.
chamomile-tea.tier_note: C fits: effects are consistent in direction but come from few small trials with very high heterogeneity and mixed populations (some postpartum and patient groups). The evidence is largely extract-based rather than tea, and there are no objective sleep measures.
chamomile-tea.rules_note: A Tier C row that keeps when theirs and loved and clears when borrowed and weak follows the rules; this is a benefit row, not a cost row.
chamomile-tea.words_note: The summary is accurate but could add that the trials were small and inconsistent and that night-waking results were not pooled. The NCCIH allergy and warfarin cautions are not surfaced anywhere in the row, which is worth considering.
chamomile-tea.one_line: Tier C is right for chamomile tea: it may modestly help how well people feel they slept, mostly in extract trials, so keep it if someone loves the ritual, and consider adding a ragweed-allergy and warfarin caution.

sources.note: The trial's main measure was blood antioxidant capacity (FRAP), not gut health or digestion.
It tested a fibre-enriched kombucha, so the Bifidobacterium rise may partly reflect the added fibre.
Guidance page with no summary; judged only from the row's paraphrase.

kombucha-probiotic-drinks.claim_note: Tier C for gut health in healthy adults fits: one early human study, then small, short RCTs with mixed or surrogate results. The summary does not say the runner trial measured antioxidants, not gut health, so it reads as a null gut result. It also omits the one gut-relevant trial (fibre-kombucha raised Bifidobacterium). No source covers non-kombucha probiotic drinks, such as kefir or fermented milk drinks, even though the row's name includes them.
kombucha-probiotic-drinks.tier_note: Small, short, inconsistent trials using surrogate outcomes are textbook C. Nothing supports A or B.
kombucha-probiotic-drinks.rules_note: C with LOVED keep and UNUSED clear is consistent. BORROWED_WEAK in clear_when is borderline for a C row, which 'neither protects nor clears', but it is acceptable if it only applies when the drink is also unloved.
kombucha-probiotic-drinks.words_note: The summary should say the runner trial measured antioxidant and immune markers, not gut health. It should also mention the small fibre-kombucha trial that showed microbiome shifts. The 0.5%+ alcohol fact (TTB) is sourced but unused; it is worth a brief note for people avoiding alcohol.
kombucha-probiotic-drinks.one_line: Tier C is right, but reword the summary so the runner trial isn't read as a failed gut test, and either add sources for other probiotic drinks or rename the row to kombucha only.

sources.note: Fair paraphrase, though café-made broths had the highest and most variable levels.

bone-broth.claim_note: No broth trials are cited. The evidence is a lab analysis, a component-based narrative review (partly IBD and animal studies), and an indirect collagen meta-analysis showing no benefit in independent trials.
bone-broth.tier_note: Mechanism and lab data only, with no outcome trials in healthy adults, so D fits.
bone-broth.rules_note: D allows clearing when the habit is borrowed and weakly held, and protects it only when it is theirs and loved. This is a benefit row, so there is no cost-direction issue.
bone-broth.words_note: The summary is accurate. 'Fewer building blocks' holds for standardized recipes, and café broths varied. Miso as an alternative is fine, though it is salty.
bone-broth.one_line: Tier D is right: no trials show bone broth helps skin, joints or gut, so it is fine to suggest dropping it unless the person genuinely loves the habit.

hydrogen-alkaline-water.claim_note: The sources show preliminary, small hydrogen-water trials. The one meta-analysis is in overweight adults, mostly with cardiometabolic disease, and finds clinically trivial lipid changes. A narrative review finds no support for systemic alkalinisation. None establishes energy, recovery or general-health benefit in healthy adults.
hydrogen-alkaline-water.tier_note: Small, mixed, early human trials outside the target population fit C. There are some human RCTs, so D would understate it.
hydrogen-alkaline-water.rules_note: C neither protects nor clears on evidence, and keep/clear rest on ownership and use, which is consistent.
hydrogen-alkaline-water.words_note: Accurate and not overstated. It could add that the meta-analysis participants mostly had metabolic conditions, and that alkaline water's only modest signal is reflux and hydration markers, likely mineral-driven, but neither omission misleads.
hydrogen-alkaline-water.one_line: This row is sound: hydrogen and alkaline water have only weak, early evidence, so keep them only if the person loves them, and plain water is a fair swap.

sources.note: The published summary gives no caffeine-per-gram figures or human attention results, so the 31–40 mg/g number rests only on the row's paraphrase; the summary stresses that composition varies widely.
The summary confirms significant disruption at 0, 3 and 6 h from 400 mg but does not state the 'over an hour' figure or that the self-reported loss at 6 h was non-significant.

matcha-green-tea-in-the-afternoon.claim_note: Caffeine shortening sleep is well supported in healthy adults. The ~9 h cutoff was modelled for a 107 mg coffee, though, and applying it to a 60–80 mg matcha with theanine is an extrapolation; matcha itself was not studied.
matcha-green-tea-in-the-afternoon.tier_note: A meta-analysis in healthy adults could justify A for caffeine. B fits for matcha specifically, since the form was not studied and the dose is lower and variable.
matcha-green-tea-in-the-afternoon.rules_note: This is a cost-direction row: it carries UNLOVED_HABIT in clear_when and has no EVIDENCE_REGULAR in keep_when, which is correct.
matcha-green-tea-in-the-afternoon.words_note: The summary correctly ties the nine-hour figure to a 107 mg coffee. The matcha caffeine range is supported only by our paraphrase, and real products vary widely. dose_typical is missing its unit in the text, but dose_unit supplies it.
matcha-green-tea-in-the-afternoon.one_line: The row is sound: caffeine late in the day reliably costs sleep, though the nine-hour cutoff comes from stronger coffee and is only an approximation for a smaller matcha serving.

sources.note: The pooled effects match, but 'many trials small and poorly blinded' is not in the summary, which rates the weight evidence as high certainty.
The weight, BMI and waist drops match; the retracted Lebanese trial is not mentioned in the summary and cannot be verified here.
The 20% loss at 4 hours came from raspberry vinegar, while the most erosive (Bio vinegar) reached about 20% at 8 hours.

apple-cider-vinegar.claim_note: Modest glucose and weight effects are supported, but almost entirely in people with type 2 diabetes or overweight, not healthy adults. The 2025 retraction claim rests only on the row's paraphrase.
apple-cider-vinegar.tier_note: Meta-analyses are positive but in patient or overweight groups. For healthy 22 to 45 year olds the evidence is indirect, small and short, so C fits.
apple-cider-vinegar.rules_note: Keep and clear rules fit a non-protecting C row. Gummies are untested at trial doses (studied forms are liquid and some capsules).
apple-cider-vinegar.words_note: The summary is fair. Consider noting that gummies weren't what was studied and that undiluted vinegar can erode tooth enamel (lab evidence). Verify the retraction before showing it to people.
apple-cider-vinegar.one_line: Tier C is right because the benefits were shown mainly in people with diabetes or overweight. Before publishing, confirm the 2025 retraction claim and consider adding that gummies weren't studied and that undiluted vinegar can harm tooth enamel.

sources.note: The published summary reports significant disruption even at 6 h but doesn't state the self-report vs monitor split; the paraphrase is plausible and not contradicted.
No published summary, so this is judged from the row's paraphrase only.

second-or-third-coffee.claim_note: The meta-analysis of healthy adults supports the cost: total sleep −45 min, more N1, less N3, and an 8.8 h cutoff for a 107 mg coffee. The Drake RCT backs disruption even at 6 h. One caveat: the studies test caffeine doses, not an extra cup on top of morning coffee, but the extrapolation is reasonable.
second-or-third-coffee.tier_note: An independent meta-analysis of 24 studies in healthy adults, plus a consistent independent RCT, justifies A for the sleep cost.
second-or-third-coffee.rules_note: This is a cost-direction row. UNLOVED_HABIT is in clear_when and there is no EVIDENCE_REGULAR in keep_when, which is correct.
second-or-third-coffee.words_note: 'FDA calls 400 mg a day generally fine' drops the healthy-adult qualifier and the pregnancy, breastfeeding and medication caveats the source mentions. It also reads as reassurance inside a sleep-cost row. Suggested wording: 'FDA says up to 400 mg a day is generally fine for healthy adults; check with a provider if pregnant, breastfeeding or on medicines.' The rest is accurate; 'about nine hours' rounds 8.8 h fairly.
second-or-third-coffee.one_line: The tier and rules are right, but add the FDA's healthy-adult and pregnancy/medication caveat to the 400 mg line so it doesn't read as blanket reassurance.

fasting-window-skipping-breakfast.claim_note: The 99-RCT network meta-analysis found that all fasting patterns, including time-restricted eating, lowered weight versus eating freely, roughly matching steady calorie cutting. Only alternate-day fasting did slightly better. Most participants (5,862 of 6,582) had health conditions. The trials test eating windows, not breakfast-skipping specifically.
fasting-window-skipping-breakfast.tier_note: It is a large meta-analysis, but only 720 participants were healthy and certainty was mostly moderate with few long trials. B (consistent results in a narrower or mixed group) fits better than A for healthy 22–45-year-olds.
fasting-window-skipping-breakfast.rules_note: B protects when done regularly, and EVIDENCE_REGULAR in keep_when is consistent with that. This is a benefit row, not a cost row, so an empty clear_when is fine.
fasting-window-skipping-breakfast.words_note: The summary accurately says time-restricted eating matched calorie cutting and flags the mostly-condition population. The row name's 'skipping breakfast' is a slight stretch, because the evidence is on eating windows generally, which may be early or late in the day.
fasting-window-skipping-breakfast.one_line: Keep this at B: a large trial review shows fasting windows help weight loss about as well as ordinary calorie cutting, though mostly in people with health conditions and not specifically from skipping breakfast.

sources.note: No published summary is available, so this was judged only from the row's paraphrase, which the evidence_summary reflects faithfully.

water-filter.claim_note: The sources show contaminant reduction: lead in a field study, minerals in a lab study, plus CDC guidance. None measures a health outcome, so 'health benefit' is inferred from removing known toxicants rather than shown directly.
water-filter.tier_note: There are no health-outcome trials, so A or B is unjustified. For people on clean water this is close to D, but for homes with lead pipes the filter is safety-relevant. C, which neither protects nor clears, is a reasonable and safe middle. A better structure would be evidence_requires 'known contaminant such as lead pipes', with tier_otherwise D.
water-filter.rules_note: Keep_when THEIRS, LOVED and clear_when UNUSED are consistent with C. Evidence_requires 'none' hides that any benefit depends on what is in the water; consider making it conditional on contamination.
water-filter.words_note: The fits_instead line points only to the utility's yearly report. That report reflects the water system, not lead picked up from a home's own service line or plumbing, which is where filters matter most. It could falsely reassure, so it should also mention testing your own tap or checking for a lead service line.
water-filter.one_line: Tier C is fine, but change the 'fits_instead' line so it tells people to test their own tap or check for lead pipes, because the utility's yearly report can miss lead coming from a home's own plumbing.

sources.note: No published summary is available, so this was judged only from the row's paraphrase, which matches the row's evidence_summary; the 100 to 300 mg odour-study dose is not in the paraphrase and cannot be verified.

chlorophyll-water.claim_note: Per the paraphrase, skin evidence is only two ten-person topical gel pilots, and nothing tests oral chlorophyll water for skin, energy or bloating. A low tier is supported.
chlorophyll-water.tier_note: For the drink as used, the evidence is only indirect: topical gels, tiny pilots and mixed odour data. D fits, and N would also be defensible.
chlorophyll-water.rules_note: A D-tier benefit row is correctly kept when theirs and loved, and cleared when borrowed and weak or unused.
chlorophyll-water.words_note: The summary is accurate and not overstated. It could add the paraphrase's note that chlorophyll is untested in pregnancy and breastfeeding. The dose line should be verified, since the source paraphrase doesn't give it.
chlorophyll-water.one_line: The low D grade for chlorophyll water is right and Distill can suggest dropping it when it's borrowed and unloved; consider adding that it's untested in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and check the dose figure.

sources.note: Matches, but it measured any eating or drinking, not sweets specifically, and the design cannot show cause.
Sugar share was linked to arousals in a correlational analysis of 26 adults on one free-eating day; timing near bed was not studied.
Matches, but it tested a large share of calories after 9:30pm, not a dessert, and measured breathing and hormones rather than sleep lightness.

dessert-sugar-before-bed.claim_note: The sources support late eating being linked to more night waking and sugar being linked to arousals. No source tests sweets within an hour of bed, so the specific 'sweets within an hour' claim is an inference from these sources.
dessert-sugar-before-bed.tier_note: The evidence is observational plus one small crossover trial of heavy late eating. This is mixed and indirect evidence of a cost, so C is right.
dessert-sugar-before-bed.rules_note: This is a cost-direction row. It carries UNLOVED_HABIT in clear_when and does not use EVIDENCE_REGULAR, which is consistent with the rules.
dessert-sugar-before-bed.words_note: The summary is suitably hedged ('observed, not tested'). It could note that the late-eating data cover any food, not sweets, and that late eaters also slept longer. The fits_instead suggestion is consistent with Iao's finding that a longer gap before bed lowered the odds of night waking.
dessert-sugar-before-bed.one_line: Keep this row at C: late eating is linked to more night waking, but no study has tested dessert itself, so treat it as a gentle suggestion rather than a rule.

sources.note: Matches, but it is a 5-person, one-week study.
Matches, but participants were functional gut patients, not healthy adults.
Safety and timing study only; says nothing about gas, and timed charcoal did not break pill protection.

activated-charcoal.claim_note: Both gas studies found no benefit for gas or symptoms. One had 5 healthy volunteers; the other was a double-blind RCT in 34 functional patients. Juurlink supports the drug-binding statement.
activated-charcoal.tier_note: The two gas studies are tiny and short but consistently show no benefit. C fits ('small and short') and stops the item being protected. A case for D could be made, but C is not harmful here.
activated-charcoal.rules_note: C carries no EVIDENCE_REGULAR protection, which is correct. Clearing only when borrowed or unused is reasonable for a likely-useless item.
activated-charcoal.words_note: 'Mostly found no effect' slightly understates; both studies found none. The medicine-binding warning is accurate and important. It could add that people should separate it by several hours from medicines, including the pill (Elomaa used 3 h after and 12 h before).
activated-charcoal.one_line: The row is accurate: charcoal capsules don't help everyday gas in the small trials available, and the warning that they bind medicines is correct, so keep Tier C and consider adding advice to take them hours apart from any medication.

led-face-mask.claim_note: Small trials, mostly with clinic panels, show wrinkle improvement. The best independent RCT (Lee) compared against baseline, and home-device evidence is thin and of mixed quality. 'Softer fine lines with regular home use' is plausible but weakly evidenced, which fits C.
led-face-mask.tier_note: There is one independent clinic RCT, one sponsor-run trial with non-randomized controls, and reviews calling the evidence mixed, small and short. Home masks are weaker still, so C is right. The acne meta-analysis is a different claim and includes teens with acne, so it shouldn't lift the tier.
led-face-mask.rules_note: For a C row nothing should come from EVIDENCE_REGULAR, and it doesn't. Confirm BORROWED_WEAK is meant to apply to C, since C is defined as neither protecting nor clearing. cost_month_usd 20 implies amortizing a roughly $570 device.
led-face-mask.words_note: The summary is accurate and not overstated. 'Six trials found fewer spots' is supported, though those trials were in people with acne. A brief caution about photosensitizing medicines or light-sensitive conditions (AAD, label) could be added. fits_instead is reasonable general dermatology, though not sourced here.
led-face-mask.one_line: Tier C is right because LED masks have only small, mixed-quality evidence for fine lines, so keep it if the person loves it but don't protect it as proven.

gua-sha-ice-roller.claim_note: Ahn supports small (2–3 mm) contour changes, but it compared two active arms with no untreated control. Neither source measured puffiness or tested a cold or ice roller. Miyaji's blood-flow finding is brand-linked and is not an appearance outcome.
gua-sha-ice-roller.tier_note: There is one small, short RCT with no control group and one brand-linked lab study. That fits C, and it should not go higher.
gua-sha-ice-roller.rules_note: C carries no EVIDENCE_REGULAR, which is correct. Confirm that BORROWED_WEAK is meant to apply to C rows; the rules say C 'neither protects nor clears' on evidence.
gua-sha-ice-roller.words_note: evidence_for promises 'less puffy', which no source tested. The name, human_question and fits_instead centre on an ice roller's chill, but the studies used room-temperature massage tools. The summary should also say the blood-flow study was maker-linked.
gua-sha-ice-roller.one_line: Keep it at tier C. Reword the claim to 'slightly more contoured-looking face' and drop 'less puffy', because no study tested puffiness or ice rollers.

sources.note: The abstract supports scarce, small, short studies and modest benefit across 18 device studies, but does not say whether any microcurrent trial tested a different device, so that detail cannot be checked.
It reports modest benefit from small studies of home devices as a group, which the row's summary leaves out; it does not isolate microcurrent.

microcurrent-device-nuface.claim_note: Both reviews agree evidence is thin, but they describe small studies showing modest benefit for home devices generally; 'no independent trial' of microcurrent is plausible but not shown in the abstracts.
microcurrent-device-nuface.tier_note: No microcurrent-specific independent RCTs are evident, so D fits. Upgrade to C only if independent small microcurrent trials are confirmed.
microcurrent-device-nuface.rules_note: The D rules are consistent: kept when owned and loved, clearable when borrowed and weak. The row lacks any safety flag for pacemakers or implanted devices, epilepsy or pregnancy, although a source lists them.
microcurrent-device-nuface.words_note: The 'different electrical device' detail is unverifiable from the abstract, and the summary omits that reviews report modest effects from home devices as a class. The $20 monthly cost understates a $175–395 upfront price. No safety caveat appears for pacemaker users or during pregnancy.
microcurrent-device-nuface.one_line: Keep it at tier D, but soften the 'one trial' wording, note that home devices show modest effects in small studies, fix the cost, and add the pacemaker, epilepsy and pregnancy warning.

sources.note: The trial is accurate, but it tested a specific device treatment (hydradermabrasion plus serum) in 20 women aged 34 to 56, not a typical spa facial.
Brand blog with no summary; judged from the paraphrase only, and it supports only price and session length, not any effect.

facials-monthly.claim_note: One small, unblinded trial supports smoother-looking skin for one specific procedure; nothing tests generic monthly spa facials.
facials-monthly.tier_note: A single small, short trial of a narrower intervention fits C. Some might argue D for generic facials, but C does not protect, so the risk is low.
facials-monthly.rules_note: C keeps only when theirs and loved and clears when borrowed and weak, overlapping or unused, which is consistent with a tier that neither protects nor clears on evidence.
facials-monthly.words_note: The summary is honest; it could add that the trial used a device-based treatment rather than a standard facial, but it does not overstate.
facials-monthly.one_line: Keep this as tier C: the only real study tested a specific device treatment, not ordinary monthly facials, so keep facials only if the person loves them.

sources.note: No published summary, so this is judged from the paraphrase only; the row leaves out that reapplying toner every two hours added hydration.

toner-hydrating-or-balancing.claim_note: The only independent human data (Yuanxi, no summary available) found no added hydration from toner over cream alone, and the brand-funded RCT does not count; the row states this accurately.
toner-hydrating-or-balancing.tier_note: Strictly, there is one small human study, so C is arguable, but that study shows no benefit and the only positive trial is brand-funded and confounded; D is a fair practical grade.
toner-hydrating-or-balancing.rules_note: This is a benefit row, not a cost row. keep_when THEIRS, LOVED and clear_when with BORROWED_WEAK fit tier D.
toner-hydrating-or-balancing.words_note: The summary is accurate and not overstated. 'Small' is unverified from the paraphrase. 'Still a little damp' in fits_instead is common AAD advice but is not in the cited paraphrase.
toner-hydrating-or-balancing.one_line: This row is fine: the only independent study found toner adds nothing over moisturizer alone, so it is fair to suggest dropping a toner the person doesn't love.

sources.note: The summary says the devices 'can improve skin aging to a certain extent' and gives no detail on the single microcurrent trial, so the paraphrase's 'far from sufficient' and neuromuscular-stimulation detail go beyond what can be checked.

facial-plus-at-home-led-plus-microcurren.claim_note: No source tests combining the three. Component evidence is thin: small, short LED trials (some clinic-grade or sponsored), one small hydradermabrasion RCT, and almost nothing on microcurrent. That supports 'untested stacking'.
facial-plus-at-home-led-plus-microcurren.tier_note: The stacking claim has no direct study, only extrapolation from weak component evidence, which fits D. N would also be defensible, but D is fair because independent component studies exist.
facial-plus-at-home-led-plus-microcurren.rules_note: D with keep_when THEIRS/LOVED and clear_when including BORROWED_WEAK, OVERLAP and TOO_MANY_STEPS is consistent; this is not a cost row.
facial-plus-at-home-led-plus-microcurren.words_note: Minor: 'monthly facials are untested' is slightly loose, since Freedman tested a weekly hydradermabrasion series (20 women) with benefit. Also, the LED trial with real effects (Lee) used clinic devices, not home ones. Neither point overstates the case for keeping the stack.
facial-plus-at-home-led-plus-microcurren.one_line: The row is sound: nobody has shown that stacking facials, LED and microcurrent beats one alone, so D is right and asking which one to keep is a fair question.

sources.note: No summary is available, so this is judged from the paraphrase only; the paraphrase's safety cautions (photosensitizing medicines, light-sensitive conditions, dark-spot-prone skin) are missing from the row.

Brand page with no summary, judged from the paraphrase only; it supports the dose and the price range.

red-light-therapy-panel.claim_note: For skin, the only direct trial is maker-funded and its controls (largely sponsor staff) were not randomized; the AAD paraphrase says the effect may be subtle and that home devices are weaker; Grimes calls the evidence mixed. The skin claim is supported only weakly.
red-light-therapy-panel.tier_note: C is defensible: there is mixed independent literature (Grimes, AAD) plus one sponsored trial. It is certainly not A or B, and it is arguably borderline D/N given that the only direct trial is brand-funded.
red-light-therapy-panel.rules_note: Tier C should neither protect nor clear, but clear_when includes BORROWED_WEAK; confirm that this flag does not fire for C, otherwise remove it.
red-light-therapy-panel.words_note: The summary calls the Dutra exercise-performance meta-analysis 'recovery' evidence and mentions sleep and recovery even though evidence_for is skin. It also omits the AAD safety cautions about photosensitizing medicines and dark-spot-prone skin. fits_instead (morning daylight) does not substitute for a skin goal, and sun exposure works against it.
red-light-therapy-panel.one_line: Tier C is fine, but fix the summary to say the exercise evidence is about performance rather than recovery, add the dermatology caution about light-sensitizing medicines and darker skin, check that BORROWED_WEAK can't clear a C row, and pick a skin-relevant alternative instead of daylight.

sources.note: 9 of 23 biotinylated assays were affected, but the summary does not say thyroid tests specifically were among those that failed, only that they were tested.

biotin.claim_note: The sources support no benefit in healthy people and improvement only in deficiency or specific conditions. That improvement comes from 18 uncontrolled case reports, with no RCTs.
biotin.tier_note: Even for deficient people, the only evidence is case reports, which counts as anecdote and fits D rather than C. For our healthy, non-deficient users tier_otherwise N (or D) is correct, so the practical effect is small.
biotin.rules_note: Keep/clear rules match a weak tier, and tier_otherwise N for non-deficient people is appropriate.
biotin.words_note: The person-facing text leaves out the main safety point. At typical doses (10 mg), biotin can falsely skew thyroid, hormone and troponin (heart-attack) blood tests. The summary or fits_instead should tell people to stop it or tell their clinician before blood work.
biotin.one_line: Biotin rightly gets no credit for hair or nails in healthy people, but add a plain warning that it can distort blood tests, including heart-attack tests, and grade even the deficiency case as anecdote-level (D).

sources.note: 'Diets usually cover needs' isn't in the summary, and the underlying causes also included non-deficiency conditions like brittle nail syndrome, but the core finding matches.
No published summary; judged only from the row's paraphrase, which is consistent with the row.

hair-growth-gummies-biotin-blends.claim_note: No independent study tests these gummies. Biotin's hair benefit appears only in case reports of people with deficiency or another underlying condition. Drake's review did not list biotin among supplements with potential benefit.
hair-growth-gummies-biotin-blends.tier_note: N fits the product: no independent study of the blend. D (case reports only) is also defensible for biotin alone, but it carries the same keep/clear behaviour, so nothing changes in practice.
hair-growth-gummies-biotin-blends.rules_note: The keep/clear rules follow for tier N. This is not a cost-direction row, so it correctly has no EVIDENCE_REGULAR protection.
hair-growth-gummies-biotin-blends.words_note: The evidence_summary leaves out the safety-relevant point from Li 2017 and the FDA: biotin can make blood tests come out falsely high or low, including thyroid tests and the troponin heart-attack test. The summary or human_question should tell people to mention biotin before blood tests. The dose_typical field mixes a gummy count with mcg and should be cleaned up.
hair-growth-gummies-biotin-blends.one_line: The tier is right, but add a line to the person-facing text warning that biotin can throw off blood tests, including the heart-attack troponin test, so people should tell their doctor before bloodwork.

collagen-drinks-and-beauty-gummies.claim_note: Myung shows pooled benefit that disappears in independent and high-quality trials. de Miranda pools positive results without a funding analysis. Together they fit 'studies disagree.'
collagen-drinks-and-beauty-gummies.tier_note: Several RCTs and two meta-analyses exist but conflict once funding and quality are accounted for, which is classic C. It is not D, because human RCTs exist.
collagen-drinks-and-beauty-gummies.rules_note: Tier C should neither protect nor clear. Including BORROWED_WEAK in clear_when lets a C item be cleared as if it were D or N, so remove it. Keeping DOSE_BELOW_MIN, OVERLAP and UNUSED is fine.
collagen-drinks-and-beauty-gummies.words_note: The summary is fair. The fits_instead note on the sunscreen trial is accurate (about 4.5 years, 24% less aging).
collagen-drinks-and-beauty-gummies.one_line: Grade C is right for collagen, but remove BORROWED_WEAK from clear_when so a C-tier item isn't cleared like an unproven one, and double-check whether the Proksch trial was industry-funded.

eye-cream-when-you-already-use-a-moistur.claim_note: The independent review finds ingredient-level periorbital studies but no trials of eye-cream formulations. The only head-to-head test is brand-funded and confounded, because it bundled the eye cream into a five-step routine. Nothing independently shows an eye cream adds benefit beyond a face moisturizer.
eye-cream-when-you-already-use-a-moistur.tier_note: For the incremental claim, the only evidence is indirect (ingredient studies) plus one brand-funded routine RCT. D fits; C could be argued from the ingredient trials, but they don't test the claim in evidence_for.
eye-cream-when-you-already-use-a-moistur.rules_note: Keeping it when it is theirs and loved, and clearing it when it is borrowed and weak, an overlap, or unused, is consistent with Tier D and a benefit-direction row.
eye-cream-when-you-already-use-a-moistur.words_note: The summary is accurate and modest. The human question correctly prompts a check on whether the jar contains an active such as a retinoid that the moisturizer lacks. The ring-finger tip matches the AAD paraphrase.
eye-cream-when-you-already-use-a-moistur.one_line: This row is sound: there is no independent proof that an eye cream beats your moisturizer, so suggesting a drop is fine unless the person loves it or it contains an active like a retinoid that their moisturizer lacks.

massage-membership-massage-envy-squeeze.claim_note: Both meta-analyses support short-term anxiety relief and less post-exercise soreness. The trait-anxiety and depression effects came from mixed populations that were partly clinical, and the soreness benefit applies only after exercise.
massage-membership-massage-envy-squeeze.tier_note: B fits: two independent meta-analyses agree, but the trials are small, often low quality, partly in clinical groups (Moyer is from 2004), and the effects are mostly short-term.
massage-membership-massage-envy-squeeze.rules_note: This is a benefit row at tier B, so keeping it via EVIDENCE_REGULAR and clearing it when UNUSED or OVERLAP is consistent.
massage-membership-massage-envy-squeeze.words_note: The summary is accurate. It could add that the soreness benefit applies after hard exercise and that the anxiety trials mixed patients with healthy adults. The question and alternative are fair.
massage-membership-massage-envy-squeeze.one_line: Tier B for massage is fair: good evidence it calms anxiety and eases post-workout soreness in the short term, so keep the membership only if the massages actually get booked.

sources.note: Guidance page; it recommends aerobic and strength activity but is not itself trial evidence that classes build strength.

class-pack-or-studio-credits.claim_note: Aerobic fitness gains from regular training in healthy 18–45s are well supported by the Milanovic meta-analysis, but no source here tests strength or group classes specifically.
class-pack-or-studio-credits.tier_note: A is defensible for aerobic fitness from regular training in this age group, gated by 'trains'. Adding a resistance-training meta-analysis would back the strength half.
class-pack-or-studio-credits.rules_note: The 'trains' gate with tier_otherwise N, EVIDENCE_REGULAR in keep_when, and UNUSED/OVERLAP in clear_when all fit a benefit-direction row.
class-pack-or-studio-credits.words_note: The summary's 'members paid more per visit than a pass' misapplies DellaVigna, which compared flat monthly memberships with a per-visit pass and did not study class packs. It also presents the study as a 'large gym study' supporting the class benefit, which it does not.
class-pack-or-studio-credits.one_line: The A tier is fine for regular classes, but rewrite the summary so it doesn't use the monthly-gym-membership study as if it were about class packs, and add a strength source or drop 'strength' from the claim.

sauna-bathhouse-membership.claim_note: Long-term heart benefit rests on one Finnish cohort of middle-aged men. The only trial is one small, 8-week RCT in at-risk adults (sauna added to exercise, measuring blood pressure). The summary states this fairly.
sauna-bathhouse-membership.tier_note: Observational hard outcomes plus small, short trials in narrower groups fit C. No RCT in healthy adults shows long-run heart benefit.
sauna-bathhouse-membership.rules_note: C neither protects nor clears; keep_when and clear_when are consistent with that.
sauna-bathhouse-membership.words_note: There are minor issues. In the cohort, 2–3 sessions a week was not significantly protective for sudden cardiac death (HR 0.78, CI crosses 1); the clear benefit was at 4–7, so dose_typical '2 to 4' is slightly generous. The 'hot bath at home' alternative is not the studied form. Consider noting the alcohol-in-sauna risk, since that is safety-relevant.
sauna-bathhouse-membership.one_line: Tier C is right because the heart benefit comes mainly from one observational study of Finnish men; consider raising the typical dose to 4+ sessions a week and adding a 'no alcohol in the sauna' note.

sources.note: This is a guideline, not trial evidence; it supports training in general but says nothing about memberships.
No published summary was available, so this is judged from the row's paraphrase only, which fits the well-known findings (about 4.3 visits a month, about $17 per visit versus $10 on a pass).

second-gym-or-studio-membership.claim_note: The sources strongly support training for strength and fitness in healthy adults. Nothing tests the extra benefit of a second membership when one already covers training. DellaVigna is about underuse of a single membership.
second-gym-or-studio-membership.tier_note: Tier A fits training itself. But this item is the SECOND membership, and its added value over one membership plus drop-in passes is unstudied. Tagging it A with keep_when EVIDENCE_REGULAR and TRAINS risks protecting a redundant $120 a month for anyone who trains. Grade the marginal item at C at most, or make sure OVERLAP always overrides.
second-gym-or-studio-membership.rules_note: keep_when includes EVIDENCE_REGULAR and TRAINS, so a person who trains at only one place could still have the unused second membership protected. The rules need to say explicitly that UNUSED and OVERLAP win over EVIDENCE_REGULAR for this row.
second-gym-or-studio-membership.words_note: The summary is fair. 'Help only if both get used' is a reasonable inference rather than a study finding. The human question and the drop-in suggestion are sensible.
second-gym-or-studio-membership.one_line: Training works, but no study shows a second membership adds anything, so don't let the strong exercise evidence lock in a membership the person doesn't use.

sources.note: Massage, immersion, contrast water, compression and cryotherapy cutting soreness matches, but 'only single recovery sessions were studied' is not in the published summary.

recovery-studio-membership-restore-remed.claim_note: Three independent meta-analyses in exercising or active adults show that cold-water immersion, compression, contrast baths and massage reduce post-exercise soreness. Effects range from slight to moderate and come from single sessions.
recovery-studio-membership-restore-remed.tier_note: Meta-analytic support could argue for A. But the effects are short-term single-session soreness changes, often small, and the membership bundles weaker modalities (cryo, IV), so B with a trains requirement is a fair call. C for non-trainers is reasonable.
recovery-studio-membership-restore-remed.rules_note: This is a benefit-direction row with EVIDENCE_REGULAR plus TRAINS in keep_when and no UNLOVED_HABIT, which is consistent.
recovery-studio-membership-restore-remed.words_note: The summary is suitably modest. It omits massage, the best-supported option, and could add that the Finnish sauna link is observational and in middle-aged men, and that IV drips carry real risks (fluid overload, infection). These are minor gaps.
recovery-studio-membership-restore-remed.one_line: The row holds up: plunges, compression and massage modestly ease soreness for people who train hard, and the B tier with a training requirement is appropriate.

sources.note: The abstract supports massage as top for post-exercise DOMS and fatigue, but the claim that 'only single recovery sessions were studied' is not stated there.

massage-monthly.claim_note: The acute effects after a session (state anxiety, HR/BP, post-exercise soreness) are supported. Lasting anxiety benefit comes from 'courses' in mixed clinical/healthy samples, typically more frequent than monthly. Soreness evidence is specifically post-exercise DOMS, not general soreness from a monthly visit.
massage-monthly.tier_note: B is defensible for acute post-session effects: two independent meta-analyses agree. It should not be read as evidence that a monthly cadence gives lasting benefit, since that dose wasn't studied.
massage-monthly.rules_note: B with EVIDENCE_REGULAR in keep_when and UNUSED/OVERLAP in clear_when is consistent. It is not a cost row.
massage-monthly.words_note: 'A course eases lasting anxiety' implies a monthly massage does this; Moyer's courses were mostly more frequent and in mixed clinical groups. 'Top for soreness' should say post-exercise soreness. The human_question and fits_instead are fine.
massage-monthly.one_line: Keep it at B, but reword the summary to say benefits are mainly short-term after a session and the soreness evidence is for post-workout recovery, not proof that a once-a-month massage lowers anxiety long-term.

sources.note: The 77-study, moderate range-of-motion gain is confirmed, but the supervised-vs-unsupervised comparison appears only in our paraphrase; the published summary says only that other moderators showed no significant difference.

stretch-studio-assisted-stretching.claim_note: A large independent meta-analysis in healthy people supports regular stretching increasing range of motion. The 'supervised a bit better, not significant' detail is consistent with the summary but not shown in it.
stretch-studio-assisted-stretching.tier_note: The general claim could reach A. B is a fair hedge for a paid assisted service, since supervision showed no significant added benefit over solo stretching.
stretch-studio-assisted-stretching.rules_note: evidence_requires 'trains' with tier_otherwise N is wrong. Stretching is itself the training, and Behm found trained state made no difference (p=0.99). Remove the requirement and TRAINS from keep_when so non-trainers who stretch regularly are still protected.
stretch-studio-assisted-stretching.words_note: The summary is accurate ('clearly' fits the moderate, highly significant effect). The human_question and home-routine alternative fit the finding that supervision and volume didn't matter much.
stretch-studio-assisted-stretching.one_line: The B grade is fine, but drop the 'needs training' condition, because stretching improves flexibility for anyone who does it regularly, athlete or not.

sources.note: The 45-minute session length and seven-week span aren't in the published summary, but the waitlist benefits on GAD symptoms, sleep and depression, the null result on worry, and the lack of blinding all match.

float-tank.claim_note: Both studies show short-term or course-level anxiety relief, but only in clinically anxious or self-diagnosed GAD adults. The single-float study had no control group, so the evidence is weak for 'lower anxiety and stress' in general.
float-tank.tier_note: C fits: one small, unblinded pilot RCT plus an uncontrolled case series, both in anxious or clinical samples, not healthy adults.
float-tank.rules_note: Keeping when THEIRS, LOVED and clearing when BORROWED_WEAK or UNUSED is consistent with a C benefit row that neither protects via evidence nor is cleared by it alone.
float-tank.words_note: Accurate and modest. 'Mostly in anxious adults' could say 'in anxious adults', since both treated samples were anxious; and the one-float result had no control group, which isn't stated. Both are minor gaps.
float-tank.one_line: Tier C is correct: float tanks have only small, unblinded studies in anxious people, so keep one if they love it, but don't treat it as proven for stress.

cryotherapy-sessions.claim_note: The Cochrane review found four tiny, high-risk-of-bias trials (64 mostly young men) with very low-quality evidence. Dupuy's broad meta-analysis suggests some benefit. Together this is weak, mixed evidence for less soreness.
cryotherapy-sessions.tier_note: Small, short, very low-quality trials with a weakly positive pooled signal fit C. There is not enough for B in whole-body chambers specifically.
cryotherapy-sessions.rules_note: C neither protects nor clears on evidence alone. Keeping when theirs and loved, and clearing when borrowed, weak or overlapping, is consistent.
cryotherapy-sessions.words_note: fits_instead calls a cold shower 'better studied', but the evidence (Machado) is for cold-water immersion at 10-15 °C for 10-15 min, not showers. Say 'a cold-water plunge' only. The summary could also note that the trials were almost all men.
cryotherapy-sessions.one_line: Tier C is right for cryotherapy chambers, but change the suggested swap to 'a cold-water plunge', since cold showers aren't the thing that was studied.

iv-vitamin-drips.claim_note: No trial in healthy, non-deficient adults supports energy, immunity or recovery benefits. The only RCT was in fibromyalgia and was null against placebo.
iv-vitamin-drips.tier_note: No independent studies exist in the target population, so N, or arguably D, is defensible. Both tiers lead to the same clearing behaviour.
iv-vitamin-drips.rules_note: An N tier that keeps when loved and clears when borrowed and weak or unused is consistent.
iv-vitamin-drips.words_note: The evidence_summary omits the safety risks the sources cite: fluid overload, heart rhythm problems, and infection or septic shock from insanitary compounding. It also calls an underpowered pilot plainly 'no difference.'
iv-vitamin-drips.one_line: The tier is right since there's no evidence IV drips help healthy people, but add a line to the summary about infection and fluid-overload risks.

retreat-wellness-weekend.claim_note: The retreat review is mostly small, poorly described, short-follow-up studies, often in ill people. The vacation meta-analysis shows gains fading after return to work. Neither supports lasting well-being gains in healthy adults.
retreat-wellness-weekend.tier_note: There are some RCTs, but they are small, heterogeneous and largely in clinical groups, and durability is unproven. That is C, not B; D would be too low.
retreat-wellness-weekend.rules_note: Tier C should neither protect nor clear. If BORROWED_WEAK means clearing on weak evidence, it applies the D/N rule to a C row; clear_when should rely only on UNUSED or non-evidence triggers.
retreat-wellness-weekend.words_note: '23 small retreat studies' slightly generalises, since most, not all, were small. The vacation evidence is about holidays, not retreats, but the summary labels it as holiday studies.
retreat-wellness-weekend.one_line: Tier C is right since retreat benefits are unproven to last, but check that the BORROWED_WEAK clear rule isn't letting a C-tier item be dropped on evidence grounds.
